newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU faces hard choice on wheat export award.
newsitem.headline: EU faces hard choice on wheat export award.

text.p: The European Union has a rare chance to drop weekly export subsidies for wheat to zero on Thursday, but traders were left guessing whether it would take the bait as worries lingered over the new crop.

Market nerves, already frayed by volatile world prices this week, were based on two main uncertainties -- whether the EU was prepared to call it a day on the 1996/97 campaign and whether it was prepared to risk early leakage of the coming harvest.
Traders bid for export refunds as low as zero at the weekly tender, apparently to secure last-minute coverage for old-crop wheat sales, exporters said.
"There are some people who need to top up cargoes. The market is certainly not long (of licences) yet," one said.

The bids followed the disappearance of 190,000 tonnes of wheat for export at a fixed zero subsidy through a daily channel this week and came amid fears the Commission would pull down the shutters on its 1996/97 campaign sooner than normal.
Weather problems in the United States and Europe roiled the world market this week and pushed up domestic French prices.
And a growing number of European officials regard the season as over after a more active export campaign in the second half of the season pushed sales well above nine million tonnes.
"The campaign is more or less finished," one official said ahead of the weekly tender.
But another potential concern for EU officials was that licences taken out now, near the end of the July/June export season, could be used for new-crop wheat up to end-August.

EU export licences are usually valid for the current month plus four consecutive months. The premium of French new-crop for August over the next U.S. next soft red winter crop is less than the difference for old-crop wheat, traders noted.
At one stage this week, new crop prices in Europe and North America briefly reached parity as the U.S. market reacted to the weekend freeze in hard red wheat growing areas.
And some traders were predicting the spread might even go into territory that would force the EU to consider bringing back last year's export tax.
The EU applies so-called negative correctives at the start of each season to stop licences from one crop year being used to ship early wheat from the next harvest.
But although the system works efficiently when export subsidies are in full swing, traders and officials said it was less clear how it would work with subsidies at or near to zero.

Current EU rules do not allow for negative export refunds. So even a corrective may not push a licence taken out at zero into negative figures for as long as it remains valid -- leaving an exporter who wished to gamble on a damaged U.S. harvest a guarantee of selling French wheat at its domestic cost.
One option for the Commission would be to signal that it was not yet in the market to sell new crop wheat by cutting off the validity for current export licences at June 30, traders said.

But that was unlikely to affect any licences awarded today as bids had already been filed under present rules, one exporter said. The EU took similar action to restrict the validity of flour export licences last week.
Most traders and officials said a new export tax, while part of the EU's arsenal, seemed less likely immediately as world prices had fallen back and the end-of-season timing was wrong.
EU delegates who discussed a trade issue for malting barley in Brussels on Thursday morning were given no hint of any immediate decision to reintroduce taxes, one source said.
